match.reason: Neither bank point covers crime statistics, how often offences occur, or the harm an offence causes to victims and the community; they teach crime categories and summary versus indictable offences instead.

draft.title: Trends and impact of an offence
card: Crime statistics count how many offences are recorded over a period. In Victoria, the Crime Statistics Agency publishes them.
A trend is the pattern in those counts over time, such as a rise or fall across several years. Comparing Victoria with other places shows whether a trend is local or wider.
Statistics only count offences that are recorded. Some offences are never reported, so the real number of offences may be higher than the figures show.
The impact of an offence is its harm. It can reach the victim, their family and friends, and the wider community, for example through injury, lost money, fear or the cost of services.
draft.remember: Statistics show how often an offence is recorded. Impact shows how far its harm spreads.

a.q: Recorded car thefts in a Victorian city fall each year for five years. What does this describe?
opts: A trend in the recorded offence
The impact of the offence on victims
A defence to the offence
The harm done to the wider community
a.why: A pattern in recorded counts over several years is a trend. Impact is about harm to people, which a count alone does not show.
a.clue: Look at the pattern across the years.

b.q: Dan's shop in Bendigo is burgled. He loses stock, his staff feel unsafe, and nearby shops pay for extra security. What does this show about the offence?
opts: Its harm reaches beyond the direct victim
Its harm is limited to the person targeted
Its harm can be measured only by crime statistics
Its harm falls only on people who report it
b.why: Staff and nearby shops are affected as well as Dan, so the impact reaches families, workers and the community. Statistics count recorded offences but do not show this wider harm, so the third option is wrong.
b.clue: Count everyone affected, not only Dan.

a.best: A trend in the recorded offence

b.best: Its harm reaches beyond the direct victim

problems.detail: Why (b) says 'the third option is wrong', but options are shuffled and the third option shown is the correct one. Students could read the why as rejecting the right answer; it should name the option by its wording.
Why (b) says the impact reaches 'families', but the scenario mentions only Dan, his staff and nearby shops, not families.
All three wrong options use 'only' or 'limited', and the right option is the only one without an absolute word. A student could pick it by spotting that pattern without knowing the idea.

b.q: Dan's shop in Bendigo is burgled and police record it. He loses stock, his daughter who works there feels afraid, and nearby shops pay for extra security. Which part shows harm to the wider community?
opts: Nearby shops paying for extra security
Dan losing stock from his shop
Dan's daughter feeling afraid at work
Police recording the burglary
b.why: The nearby shops were not targeted, yet they bear a cost, so the harm has spread to the wider community. Dan losing stock is harm to the direct victim, and his daughter's fear is harm to his family. Police recording the burglary adds to the statistics but is not itself a harm.
b.clue: Find the people who were not targeted and are not Dan's family.
